entities.label: Idea
entities.summary:
Monotheism in Islam is the central monotheistic concept of a single, indivisible god that has shaped the Islamic faith since its inception. The Quran, revealed to the Prophet Muhammad in the 7th century CE, presents a unified concept of God (Allah) as the sole deity, emphasizing monotheism's significance in Islam's early history. This doctrine has been a cornerstone of Islamic theology, influencing the development of the faith's jurisprudence, art, architecture, and culture. The concept of Tawhid, or the oneness of God, has been a central tenet of Islam, shaping the Islamic world's spiritual, intellectual, and social landscape.

Monotheism in Islam has had far-reaching consequences, including the unification of the Arabian Peninsula under the Rashidun Caliphate and the spread of Islam throughout the Middle East and North Africa. The Islamic Golden Age, which spanned from the 8th to the 13th century CE, saw significant scientific, philosophical, and cultural advancements, all of which were influenced by the monotheistic principles of Islam.

The legacy of monotheism in Islam continues to shape the modern world, with the faith remaining one of the largest and most influential religions globally. The concept of a single, indivisible God has inspired countless works of art, literature, and music, and continues to be a source of spiritual guidance and inspiration for millions of Muslims worldwide.

The Hadith, a collection of sayings and actions attributed to the Prophet Muhammad, emphasizes the importance of monotheism, stating, 'There is no deity except Allah, the One, the Uncompromising' ('Lā ilāha illā'llāh, al-Muḥyī, al-Muqīm'). This affirmation of monotheism has been a cornerstone of Islamic worship, shaping the daily prayers, rituals, and devotional practices of Muslims worldwide.
